sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Using AI competently is one skill. Using it responsibly is another. This lesson covers the main ethical dimensions of AI use that you'll encounter as a regular user — not as a philosopher or a policy expert, but as someone who will use these tools daily. By the end you'll understand the key considerations around copyright, disclosure, bias, and environmental cost, and you'll have articulated your own position in writing.

## Copyright and Ownership

When you use AI to generate text, images, or code, a legitimate question arises: who owns the output?

The current legal position in most jurisdictions is that AI-generated content without meaningful human authorship is not protected by copyright — it falls into the public domain. This matters in two directions.

**What you generate:** If you ask Claude to write a complete article and publish it unchanged, you may not hold copyright on that article. The practical implication is that if intellectual property ownership matters to you (for commercial work, publishing, etc.), you should meaningfully edit and add to AI-generated content — that editorial work is where your authorship lies.

**What the AI was trained on:** The models themselves were trained on data that included copyrighted text, images, and code. This is an active legal and ethical debate. Several lawsuits are in progress as of 2025, and the law is genuinely unsettled. The key practical point: don't use AI to reproduce large excerpts from copyrighted sources verbatim. Summaries, paraphrases, and transformative uses are on much safer ground.

**For code specifically:** AI coding tools like Copilot and Claude Code are trained on open-source code. Some of that code has licenses (MIT, GPL, Apache) that place conditions on reuse. This doesn't mean you shouldn't use AI coding assistance — the risk of accidentally reproducing a specific licensed snippet is low, and the tools have filters in place. But if you're building commercial software, be aware that the legal situation is not fully resolved.

## Disclosure and Authenticity

Should you tell people when you've used AI to help produce something?

There's no single universal rule, but the emerging norms are reasonably clear:

**Academic work:** Most educational institutions now have explicit AI policies. When in doubt, assume disclosure is required — the cost of disclosing when you didn't need to is zero; the cost of not disclosing when you should have can be severe.

**Professional content:** Content published under your name — articles, reports, social media posts — creates a reasonable expectation that it represents your thinking. Using AI as a drafting or editing aid is widely accepted. Using AI to generate your opinions wholesale is a different matter. The question to ask yourself: *would the reader feel misled if they knew how this was made?*

**Personal communications:** Using AI to help draft an email or refine a difficult message is ethically uncontroversial — people have always used spellcheckers, writing guides, and colleagues to improve their communication. The line blurs when AI is producing emotional content you're representing as your own genuine feeling.

The framework that holds up under scrutiny: **AI as a tool, you as the author.** The AI helps you express your ideas more clearly, research more efficiently, and work faster. You remain responsible for the ideas, the accuracy, and the intent behind whatever you publish.

## Bias and Fairness

AI models learn from human-generated data, and human data contains human biases — cultural, historical, political, demographic. This means AI systems can perpetuate or amplify those biases, sometimes in subtle ways.

Common manifestations:
- Image generation tools defaulting to certain demographics when asked to generate "a doctor" or "a CEO"
- Sentiment analysis tools performing better on text written in certain dialects
- Hiring tools trained on historical data recommending candidates who match historical patterns, regardless of merit
- Language models having richer, more nuanced knowledge of subjects heavily covered in English-language internet text

As a user, the practical implication is: treat AI outputs involving people with the same critical eye you'd apply to any system. Don't assume that because an AI made a recommendation it's therefore neutral or objective. Objectivity has to be earned and verified — it isn't automatically conferred by automation.

**Environmental cost:** Training a large AI model requires significant energy — estimates for GPT-4-scale training runs range from hundreds to thousands of megawatt-hours. Inference (using the model) is much more efficient per query, but at scale it adds up. This doesn't mean you shouldn't use AI tools — the same is true of cloud computing generally — but it's worth being aware of. The AI industry is investing heavily in efficient hardware and renewable energy; the picture in five years will be meaningfully different from today.

## Acceptable Use Policies and Your Responsibilities

Every major AI provider publishes an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) — the rules governing how you can use their tools. Anthropic's AUP is publicly available at [anthropic.com/legal/aup](https://anthropic.com/legal/aup). It's worth reading — not because you're likely to accidentally violate it, but because understanding the boundaries of acceptable use is part of using the tool responsibly.

The broad categories prohibited across most AI platforms:
- Generating content designed to deceive (deepfakes for fraud, impersonation)
- Creating cyberweapons or detailed instructions for real-world harm
- Generating child sexual abuse material
- Undermining oversight of AI systems
- Facilitating illegal discrimination or harassment

Most users never come anywhere near these limits. But the AUP also encodes something important: the company's view of what AI should and shouldn't be used for. Reading it is a shortcut to understanding the values built into the tool you're using.

The **Partnership on AI** (partnershiponai.org) is a multi-stakeholder organisation that includes Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and civil society groups. Their publications on responsible AI development represent the current best-practice thinking across the industry — more nuanced and less marketing-inflected than individual company statements.

sections.title: Policy Reading + 3 Personal Commitments
sections.content:
This workshop has two parts: reading and writing. Set aside about 20 minutes.

**Part 1 — Read (15 minutes)**

1. Read Anthropic's Acceptable Use Policy at [anthropic.com/legal/aup](https://anthropic.com/legal/aup). You don't need to memorise it — read it the way you'd read a thoughtful document: looking for the reasoning, not just the rules. What does it tell you about what Anthropic thinks AI should be for?

2. Browse the Partnership on AI's website at [partnershiponai.org](https://partnershiponai.org). Find their "ABOUT ML" guidelines or any recent publication on responsible AI. Read the summary or first few sections.

As you read, keep a running note of anything that surprises you, challenges you, or that you disagree with. These reactions are the material for Part 2.

**Part 2 — Write your 3 personal commitments (5 minutes)**

In your notes (or in the `my-ai-rules.md` file you created in lesson 1-5), write exactly 3 personal commitments for how you will use AI. Make them specific enough to be actionable — not "I will be ethical" but a concrete behaviour you can check yourself against.

These are just for you. There's no right answer. The goal is to think it through and write it down — which forces more rigour than just thinking about it.

**Some examples to spark your thinking (don't just copy these — write your own):**
- *"I will always disclose to my readers when I use AI to generate or substantially draft content I publish."*
- *"I will never use AI-generated text in an academic submission without explicit instructor approval."*
- *"I will check one factual claim per AI response before acting on it."*
- *"I will not use AI to produce content I know to be misleading, even if it's technically permitted."*
- *"I will keep a log of significant AI-assisted work so I can be transparent about it if asked."*

Write the three commitments. Save the file. This is your ethical foundation for the rest of the course.

sections.question: You use Claude to draft an article you publish on your professional blog. You edited the draft substantially, added your own examples, and the final piece reflects your real views. What is the most defensible ethical position here?
options: Never acceptable — any AI assistance in published work is unethical
Acceptable with no disclosure needed — everyone uses writing tools
Acceptable — AI was a drafting tool and you are the author — but disclosure is worth considering, especially if your audience would care
Only acceptable if you declare exactly which sentences Claude wrote
sections.explanation: Using AI as a drafting tool is widely accepted, similar to using grammar checkers or hiring an editor. When you've substantially edited the content and it reflects your genuine thinking, you are the author. Whether to disclose is a judgment call that depends on context — your industry norms, your audience's expectations, and the platform's policies. Blanket prohibition (A) is too restrictive; blanket permissiveness (B) ignores legitimate disclosure norms; sentence-level accounting (D) is impractical. The honest middle ground is C.
